rationale: B wins because it finds the operations story A leaves on the floor: "The salad chain retrofitting its own stores for conveyor belts" is a real foodservice-ops angle, not another coat of paint on the margin disclosure. A is disciplined and useful, especially "A still-unprofitable public chain is betting the path to profit runs through automation," but it stays in the obvious trio: margins, investors, labor. B also asks the sharper first-reply questions about comparability, sample size, IR, and whether the margin data is already public. Small win, not a coronation.
gaps_in_A: Misses the retrofit/buildout angle. The update says Sweetgreen will "retrofit some existing ones," but A never turns that into an operations story about cost, downtime, rollout criteria, and payback.

The headline "robot-assembled stores" and phrase "human-run ones" slightly overstate the facts. The update says automated conveyor assembly with minimal staff versus traditional stores, not fully robotic stores versus human-run stores.
The line "Is there any current news peg here? None was supplied" is too cute and partly wrong. The expansion plus newly shared margin data is the peg; what is missing is an external newsjacking peg.

The labor angle is valid, but "what automation does to fast-casual jobs" risks outrunning the evidence unless staffing-hours data appears. A flags that, but the headline still sounds broader than the fact base.
gaps_in_B: "people line" is loaded and imprecise. Traditional Sweetgreen stores are not literally a "people line" opposite a robot line; that phrasing invites a cheap story the facts do not quite support.

"That's the decision other operators are weighing right now" invents a category-wide live dilemma. It may be true, but it is not in the update, and this exercise does not reward confident industry cosplay.

The data angle and contrarian angle overlap. "still isn't profitable" appears in the first headline, then returns as "betting on machines before it has proved the business"; both work, but the distinction needs tighter separation.

"The prevailing belief is that a company that hasn't reached profitability should be conserving capital" is an asserted market premise, not a supplied fact. It needs analyst or investor evidence before it becomes a pitchable counterposition.
